results.summary: This is a 12-bit differential (11-bit single-ended) successive-approximation-register ADC implemented with custom metal-fringe capacitors and a calibrated comparator. It samples the input for two clock cycles, performs a binary search conversion over 16 cycles, and outputs the result in two 6-bit halves on the DATA pins synchronized to CLK_DATA. The design supports both differential and single-ended modes, with an offset calibration feature enabled by EN_CAL_OFFSET. Silicon tests show it works at 10-20 MHz but with noticeable noise and missing codes, requiring averaging for accurate results.

This is a 1-to-3 router that directs 3-bit data packets to one of three outputs based on control signals. It accepts data_in, pkt_valid, and read_enb signals, and provides data_out, vld_out, err, and busy status. The documentation is minimal, stating only that it routes data to three directions and suggesting to give input to data_in. No external hardware or detailed testing procedure is described.

This is a real-time motor controller designed to drive stepper motors with precise timing between steps. It interfaces with an RP2040 via SPI for register programming and control, and provides 8 motor control outputs along with general-purpose I/O. External hardware includes a 28BYJ-48 stepper motor with a ULN2003 driver, and optionally a second motor. The design is intended for use with the Tiny Tapeout demo board, and MicroPython support is planned but not yet available.

This is an implementation of the classic SIMON memory game, where the user must repeat an ever-growing sequence of button presses. It uses four buttons for input and a 7-segment display to show the current sequence length or an 'L' upon losing. The design requires a Digilent PmodBTN for button input and has been tested successfully by multiple users. It is a simple, self-contained game with no additional external hardware beyond the Pmod.

This project implements a Serializer and Deserializer (SerDes) module that converts 8-bit parallel data to a 10-bit encoded serial stream and back. It uses 8b/10b encoding for data integrity and includes control signals for enabling serialization, deserialization, and data latching. The design is purely digital and requires no external hardware, making it suitable for integration into larger systems. The documentation is thorough but lacks silicon test results.

This is a video and audio player that reads binary 80x60 pixel video and PCM/PWM audio data from an external SPI NOR flash chip and outputs it as 640x480 VGA with audio. It supports configurable audio type (PCM or PWM), VGA PMOD type, and pixel colors via input pins. External hardware includes a VGA monitor, a Tiny VGA PMOD, an SPI flash chip (W25Q128JVSSIQ), and for PWM audio an external DAC. The design is notable for playing the 'Bad Apple' video and demonstrating complex data streaming from flash.

This is a simple Pong game where the ball is represented by an image of the Polish pope, output over VGA. It supports two players via button inputs or an AI opponent, selectable by a pin. The design requires external hardware for VGA digital-to-analog conversion, a VGA monitor, and buttons for player input. The game logic runs once per frame during vertical sync, and it outputs one pixel per clock cycle.

This is a configurable digital clock that defaults to 20 MHz but can be set to 10, 12, or 14 MHz via input pins. It supports display of minutes or hours on a 2-digit 7-segment display, with an option for 4-digit mode, and includes an Arduino mode. External hardware includes a PMOD 2-segment display (and possibly a 4-segment display). The design is simple and intended for basic timekeeping with adjustable speed for setting.

This is a small System-on-Chip (SoC) built around DuckCPU, a custom 8-bit CPU inspired by the Zilog Z80 and Sharp LR35902. It includes peripherals such as UART, SPI, and GPIO, and uses a reserved SPI interface for external flash and RAM. The design is intended for learning purposes and requires external SPI flash and RAM ICs, as well as a USB-to-UART circuit for programming via a bootloader. Detailed documentation is promised after tapeout.

This project displays a bouncing Tiny Tapeout logo on a 640x480 VGA screen, mimicking a DVD screensaver. It includes options to tile the logo across the screen and enable color output via input pins. The design requires a TinyVGA PMOD and a VGA monitor, and has been tested successfully by multiple users. It is a simple visual demo with no additional external hardware.
